To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the PT1-Cla2+ Gla-domain binds to a membrane containing anionic phospholatidylserins through two dipalmytoyl phosphatidylsersine lipids.
the binding of the PT-Ca2+ protein to a membrane containing DPPS is driven by a combination of electrostatic and hydrophobic interactions and the presence of two binding sites.

the binding site of the PT1 Gla domain for a single DPPs is well-defined in the presence of a lipid membrane, and that there is a second binding site for a DPPS that is located on the opposite face and is formed by the PT1 G1a domain, Ca2+, and Lys11.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the binding of the PT-Ca2+ to a lipid membrane.
the binding of the PT-Ca2+ to anionic phosphatidyl serine in a lipid membrane.
the binding of the vitamin K-dependent protein PT1-Ca(2+) complex to anionic phosphatidyl serine (PS) in a dipolarphosphatidycholine (DPPG) membrane.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the PT1-Cla complex binds two DPPS molecules with a free energy of binding around -22 kcal/mol, and this is the most probable explanation for the observed binding of the PT-Ca2+ to the membrane.
the Gla domain in the presence of a calcium ion binds to a membrane containing two phosphatidyl serines.
the Gla domain binds through two DPPS molecules, one on each side, to the PT1-Cla2+ complex.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
a PT1-Ca complex binds two DPPS lipids with an overall energy of -20.3 kcal/mol.
the PT1-CA2+ Gla domains bind to a DPPS bilayer via the first binding site with two Ca2+ ions and to a DPPC bilayer via the second binding site with one Ca2+ ion.
the PT1-Cla domain binds to the lipid membrane through two dipolar DPPS headgroups.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the PT1-Cla2+ complex can bind to a single anionic lipid in a DPPPC lipid membrane.
the PT1-CA2+ complex can bind two DPPS molecules simultaneously.
the Gla domains of vitamin K-dependent coagulation factors are capable of binding to a membrane through a single phosphatidyl serine.
